🌱 Soil Profile & Health — SoilGrids v2.0

Profile estimates are sampled from ISRIC SoilGrids public maps at each stored mill coordinate (250 m grid, 0–5 cm mean). These are modeled estimates, not field or live sensor measurements. Add/edit coordinates in the Mills tab. SoilGrids does not provide phosphorus, potassium, or organic matter; enter those only from a laboratory test. Its total-N map is not a direct measure of plant-available nitrogen. Soil organic carbon is shown separately and must not be treated as organic matter. The current public map backfill has values for 18 of 19 default mill coordinates; one coordinate returned no profile pixels, so its chemistry/profile fields remain blank.

Use as a screening tool: these are 250 m map-cell estimates at stored coordinates, not field measurements. Check each coordinate and confirm with a local laboratory before applying lime or fertilizer. Open-Meteo moisture is separate volumetric water content (%).

🌾 Soil Fertility Index

One 0–100 score per mill that combines organic carbon, pH, nitrogen, CEC, texture and — where you have lab values — phosphorus and potassium. Each indicator is scored 0–1 against cane-growing ranges, then weighted. If an indicator is missing, the score uses the rest and the coverage shows how much of the weight was available.

🧫 Lab Results — Import & Trends

Import lab certificates in bulk (CSV), keep every test per site, and see whether pH and carbon are rising or falling over the seasons. Lab values replace the modeled estimates for the same property. Compare tests from the same lab and method — lab-to-lab differences can be as large as a real change.

📡 Sensor Monitoring & Verification — by zone

Field sensor readings over a season, checked and summarised per growing zone. Readings come from a CSV, a live JSON feed or manual entry. Bad readings (out of range, stuck sensor, spikes) are flagged and left out. A mill's soil data counts as verified only when enough sensor days exist and the sensor pH agrees with the map/lab value. Moisture comes from sensors only when you load them — the map moisture is a modeled estimate.

How verification works
  • Quality control: moisture 0–70 %, temperature 5–60 °C, EC 0–20 dS/m, pH 2–11. A run of 6+ identical values marks a stuck sensor. A value far from that location's median (5× robust spread) is a spike. Flagged readings are excluded.
  • Enough data: at least 10 valid readings on 5+ different days spanning 14+ days in the chosen period.
  • Verified: enough data and sensor median pH within 0.5 of the map/lab pH. Check: 0.5–1.0 apart. Conflict: over 1.0 apart — the map value is probably wrong for that site; take a lab sample.
  • Monitored: enough data but no pH sensor, so only moisture/temperature are tracked.
  • N, P and K from low-cost probes are indicative only and are not used for verification.
  • Moisture band: below 15 % is dry, above 40 % is very wet (same classes as the map). Zone figures use the median of each mill's own median, so one busy sensor does not dominate.

⚠️ Zone Early Warning

Checks the next 7 days of rain and evaporation (Open-Meteo) against the last 14 days, mill by mill, then rolls up per growing zone. If your real sensor readings exist for the last 7 days, they raise or confirm the warning. Demo sensor data is never used. High warnings are added to the Alerts tab automatically (once per zone, risk and day).

How the warnings are decided
  • Water balance = forecast rain (7 d) minus 0.9 x evaporation (7 d). Cane at mid-season uses roughly that much.
  • Drought: High if the balance is -20 mm or worse and the last 14 days brought under 25 mm, or if sensors read dry (median under 15 %) and the balance is negative. Watch if the balance is -12 mm or worse, or sensors read dry.
  • Waterlogging: High if 3-day rain is 60 mm or more (50 mm on heavy clay) or 7-day rain is 120 mm or more, or sensors read very wet (over 40 %) with 25 mm or more due. Watch at 40 mm in 3 days or 90 mm in 7.
  • Harvest and cane delivery: Watch when a day of 30 mm or more is forecast in the next 3 days at a third or more of the zone's mills.
  • These are rules of thumb for planning, not crop-model output. Tune them with your agronomists. The actions are general practice, so confirm locally.

🔬 Soil Spectroscopy → Carbon, Clay, pH & Variety Fit

How this helps pick the right variety
A variety is matched to a field by altitude, rainfall and soil. Lab soil tests are too slow and costly to cover every farm, so most advice falls back on a regional average. A soil spectrometer scans a sample in about a minute; once calibrated, one scan predicts organic carbon, clay, sand, pH and CEC. Those turn into a soil type per field (clay, loam, sandy loam, Nitisol, Vertisol) that feeds the Variety Advisor, plus warnings: low-carbon or sandy fields favour drought-hardy, good-ratooning varieties and need extra care; acid soils need lime first.
Carbon by itself does not choose a variety — it improves the soil input and flags risk. Altitude, rainfall, smut and maturity still decide. The model must first be calibrated on your soils (steps below).
📋 How to build the calibration (sampling & lab protocol)
  1. How many: aim for 100–200 samples, 30 absolute minimum. Cover every zone and soil type and the full range from poor to rich soils; a model only predicts soils like those it learned from.
  2. Field sampling: 0–20 cm, a composite of ~5 cores per sample point; avoid headlands and freshly fertilised strips; record GPS, mill, land use and date.
  3. Preparation: air-dry, crush, sieve to 2 mm. Use the same preparation for calibration and routine samples.
  4. Lab values (one lab, one method): SOC by dry combustion (preferred) or Walkley-Black (note which); clay/sand by hydrometer or pipette; pH in water 1:2.5; CEC by ammonium acetate.
  5. Spectra: same instrument and settings throughout; scan each sample 2–3 times (repack between) and average; check the white reference regularly. Vis-NIR (about 350–2500 nm) or mid-IR both work; mid-IR is usually more accurate for carbon.
  6. Check honestly: this tool cross-validates; also keep 25–30% of samples aside and test them with Spectra to predict (include the lab columns) to get an independent score. Trust SOC when RPD is 2 or more.
  7. Keep it valid: re-calibrate for a new instrument, new soil type or new preparation. A spectral lab such as ICRAF's in Nairobi may be able to scan samples and share a regional spectral library; confirm with them.
Prefilled with each mill's location — replace with the real sample GPS.
1 · Calibration file (CSV)
One row per sample: ID, lab columns (SOC, and optionally Clay, Sand, pH, CEC), then one column per wavelength (header = the wavelength).
2 · Spectra to predict (CSV)
Same layout. No lab columns needed — if you include them, the tool scores itself on these samples (independent validation).
🧪 Which samples go to the lab?
Scan many soils, then pick the few that best cover the range. Upload the scanned spectra (CSV, same layout); lab columns are not needed. Samples already in your library count as measured.
📚 Spectral library
Keeps every lab-tested spectrum so the model can be rebuilt as it grows. Stored in this browser — export a copy to back it up or share it.
🎯 Local check & correction
New area or a different scanner? Upload 10–15 spectra with lab values from there. The tool tests the model on them and, only if it helps, fits a correction.

📊 Supply-Consumption Gap

National Production + Imports vs. National Consumption, for every year entered. This is the same method ISS Africa/ENACT use to estimate smuggling scale: a persistent shortfall (consumption exceeding official supply) is evidence undeclared sugar is entering the market somewhere. A surplus isn't itself proof of anything — could mean stockpiling, exports, or the consumption figure needs updating.

☁️ Supabase Cloud Sync

⚠️ Cloud sync not configured — data only exists in this browser. Set up Supabase to sync across devices and share with KSB stakeholders.

One-time setup (5 minutes):
1. Go to supabase.com → log in with your existing account → New Project
2. Once created, go to SQL Editor and run this once:
CREATE TABLE ksb_store (
  key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  value TEXT NOT NULL,
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
ALTER TABLE ksb_store ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY "anon_all" ON ksb_store FOR ALL TO anon USING (true) WITH CHECK (true);
3. Go to Project Settings → API → copy your Project URL and anon public key
4. Open this HTML file, find the two lines at the top of the <script>:
const SUPABASE_URL = ''; and const SUPABASE_ANON = '';
5. Paste your values, save, and redeploy to Netlify — done.
The anon key is a public read key — safe to embed here (Row Level Security controls access).

🦙 Ollama Local AI Brain

Run AI entirely on-premise. Ollama hosts LLMs locally (llama3.2, mistral, gemma2, etc.) so no sugar-sector data ever leaves KSB's network. Falls back to Gemini cloud only if local AI is offline.

One-time setup (KSB IT / Intern):
1. Install Ollama: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
2. Pull a model: ollama pull llama3.2
3. Start with CORS (so the browser can reach it):
OLLAMA_ORIGINS=* ollama serve
4. If dashboard is on Netlify and Ollama is on a LAN PC, enter that PC's IP above (e.g. http://192.168.8.101:11434)
Data never leaves your network. The dashboard sends article text to your local machine, not to Google/x.ai.

☁️ OpenRouter Cloud AI (Primary Backend)

OpenRouter provides unified access to Gemini, Claude, Llama, GPT-4o and 200+ models via one API key. This is the default cloud AI for Sugartrends when Ollama is offline. Your key is stored in browser localStorage — never transmitted to our servers.

How it works:
1. Your API key is saved in localStorage only — it never hits our Netlify functions or Supabase.
2. The dashboard calls OpenRouter directly from your browser (CORS-enabled).
3. If OpenRouter fails, it auto-falls back to Gemini (Google AI Studio key).
4. If you also run Ollama locally, local AI takes priority for complete data privacy.
Priority: Ollama (local) → OpenRouter (cloud) → Gemini (fallback). All three can coexist.

💾 Local Backup & Restore

Everything in this dashboard lives in your browser only — there is no shared server. If you clear browser data, switch devices, or the browser's storage gets reset, everything is lost unless you've backed it up. Download a full backup regularly, especially before clearing browser data.

💬 Ask About Varieties

Ask in plain language — answers come directly from the same 36-variety KEPHIS dataset used above, not a generic AI model. Try: "which variety is best for Nzoia", "what is smut tolerant and high yield", "compare CO 421 and KEN 00-13", "which varieties mature fastest".

🌱 Planting Window Advisor

Soil Data tells you what the ground is like right now. This looks forward — a 10-day rainfall/evapotranspiration forecast plus current soil temperature, read against real cane-establishment agronomy, to flag whether the coming days are safe to plant into.

Forecast: Open-Meteo (free, public). This is a screening signal from public forecast data — re-check closer to your actual planting date and use it alongside field judgment, not instead of it.

🚦 Early Warning — Border Crossing Risk

Auto-refreshes every 30 min

Traffic lights for 4 signals at every crossing: price gap, incident trend, national shortage pressure, and policy stance. Combined score is a transparent weighted average — hover any light for detail. Scores are early warnings, not predictions; the monthly log below lets you check accuracy over time.

Open this tab to compute.

🧠 Unsupervised ML — Clustering & Anomaly Detection

K-means groups crossings by shared risk profile (price gap · incidents · shortage · policy). Z-score flags crossings whose EW score is moving unusually fast — not just high, but accelerating. All computed client-side, no external model.

Opens with Early Warning panel.

📅 Monthly Prediction Log

Each time you open this tab the dashboard saves a snapshot of the top-3 predicted crossings. After 3+ months compare against real seizure news to test accuracy and adjust weights.

No snapshots yet — open this tab once a month to build a record.

🔮 Predictive Signals — Article & Alert Forecasting

Forecasts 7-day complaint/article volume and flags high-risk categories from live backend data — same linear regression + classification approach used everywhere else in this dashboard, with real guardrails: a minimum sample-size floor, non-negative clamping, and honest reliability labeling instead of a confident-looking number from too little data.

⚠️ Below a minimum data threshold, this reports "insufficient data" rather than a fabricated trend — that's expected behavior on a fresh install, not a bug. Fetch and analyze articles a few times first to build up history.

💰 Cane Price → Sugar Price Forecast

Predicts retail sugar price from a given cane price. Kenya's Sugarcane Pricing Committee sets cane price partly in reaction to retail price movements, and cane price then feeds forward into future retail prices as a cost input — a real, cited, bidirectional relationship, not an assumed one. Built from 14 individually-sourced price points (KSB announcements, USDA FAS, IEA Kenya, Statista/KNBS) — see the source table below.

🧭 KSB Data Predictive Insight

The two forecasts above are narrow (article volume, cane→sugar price). This pulls together everything else already in this dashboard — mill status, soil health, active alerts, latest production stats — and asks the AI cascade what risks or opportunities it points to over the next 1-3 months. Only uses data actually present in your dashboard right now; says so explicitly wherever something's missing instead of guessing.
